title: The Serving Chain: the architecture of a modern token system, once the weights are available
description:
A working paper, an open calculator, and a reconstructed price dataset.

When a laboratory publishes model weights, the field treats the difficult part as complete. A weight file is an artefact; a served token is a system. Between them lies a body of work that has no name, no place on an organisation chart, and no budget line — which is precisely why it goes unpriced.

This work contributes a decomposition of that work into ten layers, with an inclusion test, a cost attribution, and an argument about which layers an enterprise can acquire and which it cannot. Exactly one of the ten arrives in the download.

  • Nine layers can be acquired. One — utilisation — cannot, because it is a structural property of serving many uncorrelated tenants rather than a matter of engineering competence.
  • The cost does not sit where the discussion looks. Priced across five representative models at the precision providers actually serve, bare compute runs 0.15× to 1.80× the neocloud rate; for four of five, the silicon is cheaper than renting. Fully loaded, the same fleets run 1.7× to 8.2×.
  • It explains a common failure. A laptop demonstration exercises one layer of ten and measures latency for a single user; a production bill is set by throughput for many. The two differ by approximately two orders of magnitude.

Accompanied by: an open calculator with every input confidence-graded; a 19-point per-model API price series reconstructed from a package's git history, which the author has not found published elsewhere; and a script that regenerates every figure in the paper against pinned snapshots.

The paper records three corrections that each reduced the strength of its own argument (Appendix C). Source code is MIT-licensed; the paper and dataset are CC BY 4.0.
notes: Working paper v6. Numbers are directional and every figure regenerates via `npm run paper:figures` against the pinned snapshots in server/paper-prices.json and server/paper-gpu-prices.json. Throughput is fitted to third-party published benchmarks, not measured in-house; the paper states this and identifies the experiment that would settle it.
